This writeup details the investigation of a compromised Windows host, focusing on identifying attacker techniques using Windows Event Logs and Sysmon data. The objective was to apply MITRE ATT&CK knowledge to trace the attacker's steps, from initial reconnaissance and access to persistence mechanisms and impact.

The challenge involved analyzing various log sources, including OpenSSH.evtx, Security.evtx, and Sysmon.evtx, to uncover the full attack chain.

Asset Information

HOSTNAME SUMMARY
Compromised Windows Host A Windows endpoint that was targeted and compromised, leading to the creation of a new user, privilege escalation, and deployment of a keylogger.

Question & Answer Solutions

1. Using the firewall log image on the Desktop, what MITRE ATT&CK reconnaissance technique was used? (Format: Technique Name, TXXXX)

Active Scanning, T1595

Reasoning: Identified by searching for Syn Scan activity in the firewall logs.

2. We can see from the firewall image in Q1 that the IP address 192.168.1.33 checked to see what ports were listening on the other system. What command can we use in CMD to check which ports are listening on the endpoint? (Format: command -x)

netstat -a

3. There are ports listening on the endpoint that would enable remote connection, this could potentially make the system vulnerable to intrusion. It's time to check the logs! Which protocol and port have been used by the attacker to gain access to the system? (Format: protocol, port)

ssh, 22

4. What user account has been accessed by the attacker? (Format: Account)

administrator

Reasoning: Reviewed the OpenSSH.evtx file for successful login attempts.

5. What time did the attacker first gain access to this account? (Format: MM/DD/YYYY H:MM:SS AM/PM)

11/18/2022 9:14:08 AM

Reasoning: Executed the following PowerShell command to filter OpenSSH.evtx for EventID 4 and extract the TimeCreated and payload fields: Get-WinEvent -Path "C:\Users\BTLOTest\Desktop\Logs\Windows logs\OpenSSH.evtx" -FilterXPath "*[System[(EventID=4)]]" | Select-Object TimeCreated, @{Name='Payload';Expression={([xml]$_.ToXml()).Event.EventData.Data | Where-Object {$_.Name -eq 'payload'} | Select-Object -ExpandProperty '#text'}} | Out-String -Width 4096

6. What MITRE ATT&CK initial access technique did the attacker use? (Format: Technique Name, TXXXX)

Valid Accounts, T1078

Reasoning: The attacker gained access using a legitimate, albeit compromised, account. This falls under Valid Accounts, not Remote Services.

7. What MITRE ATT&CK credential access technique did the attacker use to gain access to the endpoint? (Format: Technique Name, TXXXX)

Brute Force, T1110

Reasoning: Brute Force is a sub-technique of T1110 Credential Access, indicating repeated attempts to guess credentials.

8. What account did the attacker create after gaining access? (Format: Account)

sysadmin

Reasoning: Filtered Security.evtx for EventID 4720 (A user account was created): Get-WinEvent -Path "C:\Users\BTLOTest\Desktop\Logs\Windows logs\Security.evtx" -FilterXPath "*[System[(EventID=4720)]]"

9. What MITRE ATT&CK persistence technique is this? (Format: Technique Name, TXXXX)

Create Account, T1136

10. What time did the attacker add his created account to the Administrators group? (Format: MM/DD/YYYY H:MM:SS AM/PM)

11/18/2022 5:15:33 PM

Reasoning: Searched for EventID 4732 (A member was added to a security-enabled local group) and examined the SID for the account being added to the Administrators group.

11. What account did the attacker delete? (Format: Account)

DRB

Reasoning: Filtered for EventID 4726 (A user account was deleted).

12. What MITRE ATT&CK impact technique is this? (Format: Technique Name, TXXXX)

Account Access Removal, T1531

13. What MITRE ATT&CK detection ID applies to the attacker's actions here? (Format: DSxxxx)

DS0002

Reasoning: Referencing MITRE ATT&CK Data Source DS0002 (Account).

14. What's the name of the compressed file that was extracted? (Format: filename.ext)

keylogger.rar

Reasoning: Searched for file creation events in Sysmon.evtx (EventID 1) related to common compression extensions like .zip or .rar: Get-WinEvent -Path "C:\Users\BTLOTest\Desktop\Logs\Windows logs\Sysmon.evtx" -FilterXPath "*[System[(EventID=1)]]"

15. What MITRE ATT&CK collection technique would this file use? (Format: Technique Name, TXXXX)

Input Capture, T1056

Reasoning: A keylogger is designed to capture user input. This was confirmed by searching Sysmon logs for process creation events (EventID 1) and command-line arguments related to input capture: Get-WinEvent -LogName "Microsoft-Windows-Sysmon/Operational" -FilterXPath "*[System[(EventID=1)]]"

16. What sub-technique of the previous answer would this file use? (Format: Technique Name, TXXXX.xxx)

Keylogging, T1056.001

17. What two files were created from this file extraction (in order of creation time)? (Format: filename.exe, filename.exe)

rundll33.exe, svchost.exe

Reasoning: Filtered Sysmon.evtx for EventID 11 (File creation) to identify the executables created by the malware: Get-WinEvent -Path "C:\Users\BTLOTest\Desktop\Logs\Windows logs\Sysmon.evtx" -FilterXPath "*[System[(EventID=11)]]"

18. What's the file path of the folder these two files created? (Format: C:\...\..\FOLDER)

atapi.sys

Reasoning: Using the same Get-WinEvent command for EventID 11, the TargetFileName field revealed the full path where the files were created: Get-WinEvent -Path "C:\Users\BTLOTest\Desktop\Logs\Windows logs\Sysmon.evtx" -FilterXPath "*[System[(EventID=11)]]" | Select-Object TimeCreated, @{Name='Image';Expression={([xml]$_.ToXml()).Event.EventData.Data | Where-Object {$_.Name -eq 'Image'} | Select-Object -ExpandProperty '#text'}}, @{Name='TargetFileName';Expression={([xml]$_.ToXml()).Event.EventData.Data | Where-Object {$_.Name -eq 'TargetFileName'} | Select-Object -ExpandProperty '#text'}} | Format-Table -AutoSize -Wrap

19. What's the name of the .sys file created by the malware? (Format: file.sys)

atapi.sys

20. What time was a registry value first set by the malware? (Format: MM/DD/YYYY H:MM:SS AM/PM)

11/18/2022 5:24:21 PM

21. What two registry values has the malware created (in order of creation)? (Format: regvalue, regvalue)

windows atapi x86_64 driver, windows scr manage

22. What MITRE ATT&CK persistence technique has the malware used? (Format: Technique Name, TXXXX)

Boot or Logon Autostart Execution, T1547

23. What sub-technique of the previous answer has the malware used? (Format: Sub Technique Name, TXXXX.xxx)

Registry Run Keys / Startup Folder, T1547.001

24. What's the name of the user on GitHub who created this malware? (Format: Username)

ajayrandhawa

Key Takeaways & Security Insights

  • •
    Get-WinEvent Behavior: The Get-WinEvent cmdlet outputs structured .NET EventLogRecord objects for standard fields (e.g., TimeCreated, Id), not raw XML.
  • •
    Custom Field Extraction: To access application-specific data (e.g., payload) nested within the <EventData> node, the .NET EventLogRecord object must be explicitly cast to an XML DOM using [xml]$_.ToXml(). This allows direct dot notation access to the raw XML structure (e.g., .Event.EventData.Data).
  • •
    Account Compromise & Escalation: The initial compromise of the administrator account was followed by the creation of a new sysadmin user and its addition to the Administrators group, demonstrating privilege escalation and persistence.
  • •
    Malware Deployment: A compressed file, keylogger.rar, was extracted, deploying executables like rundll33.exe and svchost.exe into a system-related folder, indicating a sophisticated payload delivery.
  • •
    Persistence via Registry: The malware established persistence by creating specific registry values (windows atapi x86_64 driver, windows scr manage) for autostart execution, a common technique for maintaining access.
  • •
    Account Removal for OpSec: The attacker deleted the DRB account, likely as an operational security measure to cover tracks or disrupt legitimate user access.
